A one-line generated JSON file cannot be merged as text — it must be merged as DATA. packages/bee-rs/crates/bee/src/generated/registry_payload.json is a single line, so a git conflict in it is one unresolvable hunk: whole-file ours-or-theirs, and either pick silently drops a whole side's commands. The resolution that works: parse ours, theirs, and the merge base (git show :1:<path>), diff them per command entry, and decide each entry by WHO changed it against the base rather than by which side you trust. Here that recovered main's two new verbs (bee work set/show), dropped a verb main had not yet seen retired (bee cells tier), kept our two new ones, and text-merged one description both sides had extended at the same offset. Reproduce the serialization exactly (compact separators, ensure_ascii false) and round-trip-check it against the incoming side's own line before writing, or the next merge conflicts on formatting noise.

A piped test command hides its own failure: 'cargo test ... | tail -60' exits with tail's status, not cargo's, so a red suite reports exit 0 AND the failure detail scrolls out of the kept window. This session read 'exit code 0' on a run that had a failing target. Two rules follow: always pass --no-fail-fast so cargo runs every target instead of stopping at the first red one, and never filter a test run through tail — filter through grep for '^test result|^error|^failures:' so every target's verdict survives. The repo's own recorded commands.test has the first half of this hole and is filed as a P2.

A shared fallback is only correct for the callers it was designed for. bee's resolve_mutation_target falls back to the default state record when a session has no bound lane — right for verbs that MUTATE state, wrong for the one caller that used it to READ a name to stamp on a decision. The wrong-caller cost was invisible for months: 67 decisions filed under features they had nothing to do with, which misroutes two close doors and silently denies the true owner its own D-IDs at close. The rule: when a helper resolves a fallback, every new caller must re-derive whether that fallback answers ITS question — copying a helper copies its default, and a default that means 'act here' is not the same as a default that means 'this is what this is about'. Same shape as the promoted pattern about a probe's failure direction belonging to the consequence, not the module.

A bug's first measurement is a sample, not a census. The decision mis-attribution was found by counting records stamped model-role-split and reading their text: 23. The fix's own dry-run over the whole store found 67 — the same mechanism had mis-filed decisions across release-2-11-0, uat-gate-before-merge, staging-optional and more. The sample was biased by exactly the thing that made the bug visible: I only looked where I had already been blocked. Build the general predicate, then let a dry run count it; never carry the first number into the fix's scope.

When a retired field keeps a legacy read for migration compat, every WRITE door that clears the new spelling must know the legacy spelling exists. The escalate disarm removed the new flag and considered the job done, but the compat read then answered from the old field again, so the operator control was a silent no-op on exactly the migrated records. The rule: a compat fallback read turns key-removal into an unsafe disarm — the disarm must either write an explicit override value that outranks the fallback, or the fallback must be retired first. Corollary proven by the red test: any later migration pass that derives the new spelling from the old field must treat a PRESENT key of either value as final, or it silently reverses recorded operator acts.

A parity gate that pins two copies of one command byte-for-byte is what makes a two-copy rule survivable. Adding no-fail-fast to CI alone went red in proof_gate within one suite run, because the test pins the workflows' cargo test line against commands.test verbatim — the drift was caught before it existed on main rather than months later. The general form: when a rule must live in N places (CI + config here), do not rely on discipline or docs to keep them synced; write one test that reads all N surfaces and diffs them. The pattern already existed in this repo (proof_gate) and did its job on the first try.

A validation layer that walks what the config carries still needs an arm for the key that must NOT be carried. validate_models_config was rebuilt to ask the config what it holds instead of asking a closed list what is allowed — the right fix for invented roles — but that inversion silently legalized the one key a decision forbids: a well-formed ceiling value passed every shape check because shape checks were all there were. When validation moves from allow-list to shape-driven, each existing MUST-NOT rule needs an explicit deny arm carried over, or it dissolves without anyone deciding to drop it.

SLP supervisor Phase 3 shape settled: presence is four event-sourced stores under .bee/supervisor/ (observations, interventions, presence, reports), all resolved against the CONTROL root so a linked worktree writes one store. The away/back mark has exactly two effects — it sets the report window (current_window / last_closed_window) and stamps non-urgent mailbox rows queued so they fire no notification; urgent is exempt. back is the only door that renders a WakeReport, through ensure_report_for_window, so a second back can never add a second report. Report shape is 4 headings plus at most 6 content lines (floor 8, ceiling 10), ordered by impact-if-wrong: urgent 4 > waiting-on gate 3 > escalation 2 > intervention 1, with a one-way-door decision before a reversible one; overflow ends on '+N more', never a silent drop.

SLP supervisor Phase 4 settled two shapes. (1) Health counters are DERIVED only, from .bee/cells/*.json, .bee/decisions.jsonl, the mailbox and the observation store; each carries a two-sided band, an explicit sample count, and a verdict of below-band|in-band|above-band|not-measurable, where not-measurable is first-class and never renders as in-band. Blocked-rate takes its denominator as the UNION of cells claimed and cells blocked in the window, because a swept-blocked cell has claimed_at null and blocked-over-claimed can exceed 1. The 2x-estimate counter is skip-until-present per decision ea02cb68 and reports the literal state 'no estimate recorded'. (2) silence-is-consent FAILS CLOSED where supervisor.notify fails open: only the literal {enabled:true,timeout_seconds:>=1} record turns it on, and every other read is off. Its eligibility predicate refuses by NAMED variant (gate|urgent|escalation|unknown-kind|one-way-low-confidence|not-queued|already-consented) rather than a bare boolean, and a row whose decision-log write fails stays queued rather than proceeding. The WakeReport floor moved 8 -> 9 lines to carry the fixed metrics line; the 10-line ceiling and four sections did not change.

outcome: A dispatched execution worker can die mid-cell on an API rate limit with its whole implementation and tests already on disk and nothing committed. Orchestrator recovery beats re-dispatch there: run the cell's verify against the working tree first — if it compiles and only the dependent assertions fail, finish the cell (fix, commit, bee cells finish) instead of throwing the work away. What a half-finished worker most reliably has NOT reached is the last mechanical step: sup-11 had every test written but had never declared its new verb in generated/registry_payload.json, and no test caught that because the registry contract tests only walk what IS declared.

bee dev regen does NOT re-vendor .bee/bin/bee. The binary and .bee/bin/bee.exe are gitignored (onboard/templates.rs:53-54) and explicitly protected from remove_helper (onboard/apply.rs:293); regen vendors prompts, lib, helpers and hooks only. A cell that edits a prompt template therefore closes only half the skew: prompts_match_disk (prompt.rs:72) compares BOTH source and vendored prompt against the binary's compiled-in copy, and on skew run_dispatch_prepare returns None with no Node delegate behind it since the R6 cutover. Second half, also found in the same run: a granted worktree cannot fix it either, because its .bee/bin/bee is a symlink into the main checkout and the write guard refuses to write through a symlink. Found by bln-1, 2026-08-28.

outcome: bee cells judge-record --help states the judge-verdict/1 payload as {schema, verdict, checks[], failure_signature?, fixability, confidence} but names none of the closed vocabularies, so a judge dispatch prompt written from the help alone is rejected. The real shape: each check needs id (not name), status one of PASS|FAIL, and evidence; verdict is PASS|NEEDS_REVISION (not FAIL); fixability is automatic|authority (not trivial|scoped|structural); confidence is low|medium|high. Constants at verbs/cells/judge.rs:228-234. Cost: one rejected record plus a hand-remap on bln-1, 2026-08-28.

outcome: A cell verify command whose test filter matches ZERO tests is a proof that proves nothing, and it passes green. bln-2's verify carried 'cargo test ... brief_lint' on the assumption the new module's tests would live under that path; they live in verbs::drivers::tests, so the filter matched 0 and the command still exited 0. The worker caught it and ran the seven probes by exact name instead. Rule for authoring a cell verify: a filter naming a NEW module or symbol has no tests behind it yet, so name the module the tests will actually live in, or assert the expected count. This is the running-count face of the 20260818 pattern that a green count is not evidence your new test ran.
skill_answer: changed: skills/bee-planning/references/planning-reference.md — the Test scoping section is where a cell-verify filter rule belongs, and it does not warn about a zero-match filter today

Getting an advisor-tier (fable) REVIEWER past the model guard needs the door's exact return, not a hand-assembled pair. 'bee dispatch prepare --kind reviewer --role advisor' returns subagent_type general-purpose with model fable; dispatching that pair makes the guard rewrite only the subagent_type to bee-review and KEEP fable, which is what you want. Dispatching subagent_type bee-review with model fable instead makes the guard rewrite the MODEL to opus (AO5: config is the authority, and the review tier resolves to opus), so the judge silently runs same-model as the builder and cells judge-record can only record model_independence=same-model. Learned 2026-08-28 across four judge dispatches on slp-blind-lanes: the two that used the door's return verbatim recorded confirmed, the one that hand-picked bee-review+fable did not.
skill_answer: changed: skills/bee-swarming/references/swarming-reference.md — the role rubric and escalation section is where this belongs; it tells you to use the door but never says that a hand-assembled subagent_type silently costs you the tier

outcome: A lexical rule standing in for a semantic claim invites an unbounded fix ladder, so BOUND the ladder in the cell and reduce the claim instead of adding a rung. slp-blind-lanes' citation check promised to refuse a negation strip, using a whole-sentence span rule. Round 1 judge broke it with i.e./e.g./ellipsis. Round 2 broke the fix with '(i.e.' (the set was matched by exact token equality) and with a markdown enumerator '1.'. Each round the fix was correct and each round a new written form appeared, because sentence boundaries in prose have no closed lexical definition. What stopped the spiral was not a better rule: it was writing the bound INTO the fix cell (this is the last rung; if it breaks again, reduce the claim to bare whole-sentence provenance) and correcting the over-claiming comment as a defect of equal weight to the bugs. Both judges found the holes by copying the functions out of the module, compiling them standalone and probing real strings - never by reading the tests.
skill_answer: not: this is a planning-and-judging discipline, and the nearest skill line (bee-planning's smaller-path check) is about shape size, not about bounding a guard's claim; it belongs in the pattern layer first

outcome: In verbs/blind, normalize() ASCII-case-folds the haystack BEFORE the sentence-boundary scan runs, so any downstream rule that distinguishes upper from lower case is dead code. bln-6's cell prescribed an enumerator shape of 'one to three ASCII letters, all lowercase or all uppercase'; the uppercase half can never fire, and the lowercase half swallows ordinary sentence-final words - the worker proved it by applying the literal shape and watching 14 pre-existing tests go red, because a control proposal ends 'a live one.'. The shipped shape is digits, one letter, or an i/v/x run. Rule for anyone writing a boundary rule here: check what normalize already destroyed before you write a rule that depends on it.
skill_answer: not: a module-local fact about one normalizer, with no skill line to change

outcome: PRODUCT GAP: bee cells cap --no-mistakes is unreachable from the CLI in BOTH forms, so a cap can never record the clean-run answer that bee close's mistakes door reads from the cell. Bare --no-mistakes is refused (unsupported_argument_shape) because "no-mistakes" is absent from FLAG_ALONE_BOOLEANS (verbs/reservations/flags.rs:31). --no-mistakes true is ACCEPTED, the cap exits 0, and bool_flag maps the string "true" to false on purpose (verbs/cells/util.rs:122), so trace.no_mistakes is never written. Verified 2026-09-01 on a real capped cell driven through the built binary: cap succeeded, trace.no_mistakes was absent, and the close mistakes door still blocked until bee mailbox reflect --no-mistakes ran. The unit tests stay green because they set flags.no_mistakes=true in Rust (handlers_close.rs:1906), bypassing the CLI parser — an instance of the bundle's own pattern 'a guard and its tests are one model'.
skill_answer: not: this is a CLI flag-parsing defect in the binary; no skill prose claims the flag works

Pi 0.84.4 ships three agent fan-out paths bee does not use: (1) pi.registerTool() works at runtime and Pi ships a working subagent example extension that spawns pi child processes from markdown agent definitions (pi/examples/extensions/subagent/index.ts:472); (2) the Pi SDK's createAgentSession for in-process child sessions; (3) pi --mode rpc headless children. bee's locked decision n-0d26-4a40-b51a-d18a433e42a2 says no subagent surface exists and forces every Pi dispatch through herding panes — the premise (no BUILT-IN Task tool) is true, the conclusion (herding is the only fan-out) is not. Superseding is the user's move.

Two agent binaries are installed on this machine: pi 0.84.4 (@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent) and omp 18.1.2 (github:can1357/oh-my-pi, ~/.omp paths). bee supports pi only — no .omp directory, no omp entry in RUNTIMES. omp loads legacy pi extensions (rewrites @mariozechner/* imports, shims ctx.isProjectTrusted), so an extension written to pi's narrower surface runs on both; the reverse is false. A two-target bee belt should stay inside the portable core: extension factory, on(session_start|tool_call|tool_result), registerTool, registerCommand, sendMessage/appendEntry.

Turning an opt-in into a default promotes its rough edges into the vendor's bugs. The status display had shipped for a year with a hard jq dependency that printed a RED error on every prompt when jq was missing, and a settings pointer to a script the host might not have. Both were the user's own problem while they had chosen the feature; the moment onboarding installs it unasked, both become bee's. The general rule: before flipping any opt-in to opt-out, audit every failure mode the feature can show a user who never asked for it, and make each one silent. Two more settled here: a file with more than one writer needs its backup taken once per run, not once per writer, or the backup stops being a backup; and a default that writes into a host's own config must treat an unparseable file as 'leave alone', never as 'absent', because a refusal turns one broken file into a blocked install.

Workers do not activate for three reasons, none of them the model config: (1) the session prompt's standing 'do not use the Agent tool unless the user/CLAUDE.md/a skill asks' is read as a hard block — cells pwr-1/pwr-2 record it verbatim as why no execution worker was dispatched; (2) bee herding run --ceiling defaults to 21600s and --idle-timeout only counts a dead heartbeat, so a worker that reads without editing is never stopped — sbd-3 read ~50 min, leader took sbd-3/sbd-4/sbd-5 inline; (3) dispatch prepare reports transport_ready:false outside a herdr pane although the same herding run still succeeds, so a session skips a dispatch that would have worked.

Two worker-activation fixes landed: CLAUDE.md now states outright that this repo asks for bee dispatch, so the host's 'no Agent tool unless CLAUDE.md asks' line cannot be read as a ban (it was — cells pwr-1/pwr-2); and herding.ceiling_seconds (new config key, read by dispatch prepare) appends --ceiling to the herding command, capping a pane that is busy but useless, which --idle-timeout cannot catch because a reading worker keeps its own heartbeat alive.

A release is not one command — it is a lane. scripts/release.sh refuses without BEE_DISPATCH_ID, that permit needs a dispatch at stage deployment under role deploy, and that dispatch needs an approved bee-plan/v2 plan carrying a role plan, so every release needs its own feature lane before the script can run at all. Three ordering rules fell out of doing it: --release-version is refused on --kind cell (the deploy dispatch is a NON-cell kind plus --stage deployment); the permit pins main_commit, so all bookkeeping must be committed BEFORE minting it; and the cell packet must pass cells add --dry-run before the gate, because .claude-plugin/plugin.json is a release-manifest root and the REGEN_OBLIGATION guard otherwise forces a plan-rev bump after approval. The previous release's docs/history/release-<version>/ is the template to copy, and reading it first would have avoided all of this.

read_prune_keep_set protects a cell from worker pruning only when that cell is not known-capped. Known-capped means .bee/cells/<id>.json parses and carries status capped. Both passes inside the function — the state.json workers[] receipt pass and the cell-file pass — consult the same is_cell_file_capped predicate, so they cannot drift apart. A missing or unparseable cell file still protects: the function falls open on unknown state. Before this, the receipt pass protected every cell it named unconditionally, and because nothing retires a receipt row on a normal cap, every cell ever dispatched stayed protected forever and bee state worker prune could never clean a finished cell's transient files.

outcome: A wave-ledger row is closed by a second append, never a rewrite. bee herding run appends its dispatch-time row with a blank outcome, then appends a second row for the same wave_id carrying outcome_label of the result and evidence from the report path or job log; the read-time fold makes the later row win, so the file stays append-only. An empty fleet is a closed wave (every worker reported) with at least one worker and no worker outcome of done; a wave with zero workers launched nothing, a wave with any unreported worker is still running, and a wave whose workers are all dry_run did nothing real — none of the three is an empty fleet. Before this, 431 of 437 worker rows carried a blank outcome, which degraded the occupancy read that enforces the four-slot cap to a one-hour fallback timer the code itself calls a strictly worse answer.

A test whose subject is that something must NOT happen cannot assert an exit code several paths produce. Three herding pre-flight tests asserted ExitCode::FAILURE, which the leaking path also returned, so they stayed green while spawning a real billed agent per cargo test run. The fix splits deciding from acting: preflight_receipt returns a PreflightAction from the filesystem alone, tests assert the action, and fn run is the only actor. The three sibling tests that still call run write an illegal transport into their own temp root, so a regression refuses instead of spawning.
